title: Buurtzorg – “humanity over bureaucracy” in Dutch home care
text: Buurtzorg (Dutch for “neighbourhood care”) is a home-care organisation founded in 2006 by Jos de Blok, a nurse who had become a manager in the sector. Dutch home care had been reorganised along industrial lines: tasks were cut into standardised products with time slots, planned centrally, and patients saw a different carer for each task. Nurses felt they had become executors of a schedule, many left the profession, and patients were dissatisfied. In neighbouring Germany, nearly a third of long-term-care workers leave their job within one year.

Buurtzorg started with one team of four nurses. Fifteen years later it employs more than 10,000 nurses and carers in about 900 teams and is active in more than 20 countries. Each team has at most twelve members and serves the patients of one neighbourhood. Teams are completely self-organised and self-managed: they do the intakes, plan the visits, rent their own (often modest) office, organise training, decide on recruitment after informal conversations and share out roles among themselves. Decisions are taken by consensus using a solution-oriented meeting method in which all nurses are trained.

There are no managers. About 20 regional coaches support the teams on request but have no hierarchical authority. A back office of around 50 people in the town of Almelo handles invoicing, payroll and contracts with insurers for the whole organisation; the founder insisted that there would be no HR, IT or finance department in the traditional sense. Nurses use an internal web platform to record care, share knowledge, ask colleagues across the country for advice and see their team's productivity indicators.

Care is holistic: nurses look at the patient's whole situation and aim to make the patient independent as soon as possible, drawing on the patient's family, neighbours and local professionals (and, if the patient agrees, volunteers from the community). Creativity – finding solutions on the spot – is described as a core skill. Buurtzorg's overhead costs are a fraction of the industry average, patient satisfaction is the highest in the sector, and it has repeatedly been named the best employer in the Netherlands. When a large competitor went bankrupt in 2016, Buurtzorg took over around 2,500 of its employees and integrated them with few difficulties – which de Blok attributes to the simplicity of the model and the common sense of the nurses.

De Blok remains the public face of the organisation and sums up its philosophy as “humanity over bureaucracy”. Several organisations in other sectors and countries have tried to copy the model, with mixed results.
